draft.title: Nuclear stability
card: A nucleus contains protons and neutrons. Protons are positively charged, so they repel each other with an electric force.
The strong nuclear force pulls protons and neutrons together. It acts only over very short distances, about the size of a nucleus.
In a stable nucleus, the strong force is enough to hold the nucleus together. Neutrons add to the strong force without adding to the electric repulsion.
An unstable nucleus is not held together well enough. It decays by emitting radiation, which changes it towards a more stable form.
draft.remember: The strong force holds a nucleus together. If it cannot, the nucleus is unstable and decays.

a.q: What does the strong nuclear force do inside a nucleus?
opts: Holds protons and neutrons together
Pushes protons apart from each other
Pulls electrons into the nucleus
Makes neutrons repel one another
a.why: The strong force attracts protons and neutrons to each other and works against the electric repulsion between protons. The electric force is what pushes protons apart, so it is not the strong force.
a.clue: It acts against the repulsion between protons.

b.q: A nucleus of an isotope in a lab sample emits radiation and changes into a different nucleus. What does this suggest about the original nucleus?
opts: It was unstable, as the strong force could not hold it well
It was stable, as the electric repulsion was too weak
It was stable, as only stable nuclei can emit radiation
It was unstable, as it had no neutrons in it
b.why: Only unstable nuclei decay by emitting radiation. This happens because the strong force does not hold the nucleus together well enough. Having no neutrons is not what the card gives as the cause.

b.best: It was unstable, as the strong force could not hold it well

problems.detail: The card presents instability only as the strong force being too weak against proton repulsion, and says neutrons add to the strong force without adding repulsion. This implies that extra neutrons always make a nucleus more stable. Nuclei with too many neutrons (such as carbon-14) are also unstable and undergo beta-minus decay, so stability depends on the neutron-to-proton balance, not only on whether the strong force is strong enough.

The intended answer, 'the strong force could not hold it well', repeats the card's oversimplified cause of instability. It is misleading for a neutron-rich nucleus that decays by beta-minus emission, where the problem is too many neutrons rather than too much proton repulsion.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The card and question b give a single cause of instability (strong force too weak against proton repulsion) and imply that more neutrons always help, which is misleading because neutron-rich nuclei are also unstable.

proposal.title: Nuclear stability
card: A nucleus contains protons and neutrons. Protons are positively charged, so they repel each other with an electric force.
The strong nuclear force attracts protons and neutrons to each other. It is stronger than the electric force, but acts only over very short distances, about the size of a nucleus.

Neutrons add to the strong force without adding to the repulsion, so they help hold protons together. Light stable nuclei have about equal numbers of each. Heavier ones need more neutrons than protons.

Stability depends on the balance of neutrons to protons. A nucleus with too few or too many neutrons for its protons is unstable. It decays by emitting radiation, which changes it towards a more stable form.
proposal.remember: A stable nucleus has the right balance of neutrons to protons. Too few or too many, and it decays.

a.clue: It acts against the repulsion between protons.

b.q: Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons and is stable. Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons and decays. Why is carbon-14 unstable?
opts: It has too many neutrons for its number of protons
Its protons repel too strongly for the strong force
Its extra neutrons repel each other electrically
The strong force cannot act on its extra neutrons
b.why: Carbon-14 has the same 6 protons as stable carbon-12, so the proton repulsion is no greater. The difference is its two extra neutrons, which upset the neutron to proton balance. Neutrons have no charge, so they do not repel each other electrically.
b.clue: Compare what changes between the two isotopes.

b.best: It has too many neutrons for its number of protons
